title: Quantum Illumination with Symmetry-Constrained Random Unitaries
abstract: Quantum illumination provides a quantum advantage in detecting weakly reflecting objects embedded in a noisy environment, even when environmental noise destroys most of the initial entanglement. We investigate this advantage using Haar-random probe states constrained to symmetry-resolved subspaces. Employing tools from quantum channel discrimination and asymptotic hypothesis testing, we derive the discrimination exponents associated with Haar-random probe ensembles and identify the role of symmetry in determining their performance. We show that typical states drawn from fixed-charge sectors achieve the same asymptotic quantum-illumination advantage as maximally entangled probes. In particular, we show that the effective thermal-noise suppression and the corresponding Chernoff exponent are governed by the dimension of the accessible symmetry sector. Our results reveal that the operational resource underlying quantum illumination can be generalized from fine-tuned structure of a specific probe state to the existence of a large symmetry-protected correlation subspace. These findings establish a direct connection between quantum illumination, symmetry-resolved typicality, and quantum channel discrimination, and demonstrate that near-optimal quantum hypothesis testing resources can emerge naturally from generic many-body quantum states constrained by conservation laws.
summary: The paper analyzes Quantum Illumination by replacing idealized entangled probes with generic Haar-random states constrained by symmetry. It rigorously proves that the achievable detection rate is determined solely by the dimension of the accessible symmetry sector, establishing a deep connection between quantum channel discrimination and conservation laws in many-body physics.
main_problem: The paper investigates Quantum Illumination (QI), a quantum-assisted protocol for detecting weakly reflecting objects in noisy environments, by analyzing its performance using random probe states.
main_result: The asymptotic detection advantage is governed not by the total Hilbert space dimension but by the dimension of the accessible symmetry-protected correlation subspace. This shows that generic many-body states constrained by conservation laws can yield near-optimal quantum hypothesis testing resources.
method: The analysis employs tools from quantum channel discrimination and asymptotic hypothesis testing, specifically calculating the quantum Chernoff exponent ($ ar{\xi}$) for ensembles generated by Haar-random unitaries restricted to symmetry-resolved subspaces.
model_or_system: The model is Quantum Illumination (QI), which treats target detection as distinguishing between two competing quantum channels ($\Phi_0$ vs $\Phi_1$) acting on a signal-idler probe system. The probes are generated using random unitaries sampled from the Haar measure, constrained by symmetry.
key_observables: The primary observable is the asymptotic Chernoff exponent ($ ar{\xi}$), which quantifies the exponential decay rate of the minimum error probability in distinguishing the two channels.
important_parameters: Key parameters include the dimension of the accessible symmetry sector ($d_\lambda$), the noise strength, and the probe state structure (Haar-random vs. maximally entangled).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes that the random unitaries are sampled from the Haar measure ($\mu_H$) and relies on concentration inequalities to relate the ensemble average exponent to the mean value.
figures_summary: Figure 1 schematically illustrates QI using Haar-random probes with a fiducial state, demonstrating the theoretical framework for the analysis.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first establishing QI as a channel discrimination problem (Chunk 2), then generalizing the probe states to random unitaries (Haar measure) (Chunk 3). It then develops the core theory by analyzing how symmetry constraints restrict the accessible correlations, showing that the rate is governed by the symmetry sector dimension rather than the full space dimension (Chunks 4 & 5).
why_interesting: This work provides a powerful theoretical generalization for quantum sensing protocols, demonstrating that structural symmetries inherent in physical systems can dictate fundamental resource limits, shifting focus from state preparation to subspace engineering.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Schematic of QI with Haar-random probes. For each channel use j, a Haar-random unitary Uj prepares a random signal–idler probe from the fiducial state |00⟩. The signal mode is subjected to one of two competing channel hypothe- ses Φ0 (target absent) or Φ1 (target present), while the idler is retained. Using the classical record of the sampled unitary, the receiver applies U † j and performs the final measurement. The accumulated measurement outcomes over many indepen- dent realizations are used to distinguish the two hypotheses.
